Jeepers
JEE-perz
interjection (Silent Generation slang)
American, recorded from the late 1920s, a softened form of Jesus, often in the rhyming jeepers creepers (a minced form of Jesus Christ). The 1938 popular song "Jeepers Creepers" made the phrase a national catchword, and it stayed in the mouths of children through the 1940s and 50s.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Jeepers!" said a girl in 1950 when a thunderclap shook the house; "Jeepers creepers!" said her brother when he saw the size of the dog next door. It is a funny, bouncy word, and those who said it meant nothing by it. But jeepers is a softened form of Jesus, and jeepers creepers trims Jesus Christ. That makes it worth a gentle second look, because no name in the world matters more. The angel told Joseph, "thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins" (Mat 1:21). Peter preached that "there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Act 4:12). God has given Him "a name which is above every name" (Php 2:9). The third commandment guards that name: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain" (Exo 20:7). A minced oath is not the same as cursing, and a grandparent who said "jeepers" was not blaspheming. But a name that saves is too precious to become a startled noise, even a softened one. Paul shows the better use: "whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him" (Col 3:17). A family can let the old word go quietly and teach the children to speak the name of Jesus only with love.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, late 1920s; a 1938 popular song) for a mild exclamation — a softened Jesus (jeepers creepers for Jesus Christ), innocently meant, and a reminder of the name whereby we must be saved (Act 4:12).

expand to see more

JEEPERS, interj. (American, late 1920s; also jeepers creepers) A mild exclamation of surprise or alarm. "Jeepers! That thunder about knocked me out of my chair."

Decode for families: jeepers is a softened Jesus — Grandma meant no harm, and we can keep that name for prayer.

Key Scripture

Mat 1:21 — "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins."

Act 4:12 — "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved."

Php 2:9 — "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:"

Exo 20:7 — "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain."

Col 3:17 — "And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him."

Modern Corruption

A cheerful exclamation that is, at its root, a minced form of the name of Jesus Christ; meant innocently, it is still worth setting aside out of love for that name.

expand to see more

No one who said jeepers thought of it as an oath, and many chose it deliberately to keep from swearing. That instinct was right as far as it went, and the grandparents who said it deserve no scolding.

The Christian can go further. The name of Jesus is the name of salvation (Mat 1:21), and a word built from its sound is still a use of it. Jesus taught plain speech without oaths (Mat 5:37). Retiring jeepers is a small act of reverence, and explaining why is a good lesson for children about how much that name is worth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Jesus, Jesus Christ → softened jeepers, jeepers creepers (late 1920s American) → 1938 popular song → 1940s–50s children’s exclamation.
